result.summary: Æneas tells Dido of his wanderings after Troy's fall: the horror of Polydorus in Thrace, the false oracle that sends them to Crete, the Harpies, and the prophecies of Helenus at Buthrotum. They then pass Charybdis, rescue Achemenides from the Cyclops on Sicily's coast, and Anchises dies at Drepanum.

scenes.title: Departure and Polydorus in Thrace
scenes.summary: The Trojans build a fleet and sail to Thrace. Æneas tears up bushes that bleed and hears Polydorus, murdered for his gold; they bury him and leave.
scenes.stakes: Æneas faces a cursed, violated land and an evil omen threatening the new settlement.

scenes.title: Delos and Apollo's oracle
scenes.summary: At Delos King Anius welcomes them. Apollo's oracle tells them to seek their ancient mother land, and Anchises reads it as Crete.
scenes.stakes: The exiles need a home and guidance; misreading the oracle could doom them.

scenes.title: Crete and the household gods
scenes.summary: They found Pergamia on Crete but plague strikes. The household gods appear in a dream and direct Æneas to Italy, as Cassandra had foretold.
scenes.stakes: The new city and people perish from pestilence and famine.

scenes.title: Storm and the Harpies
scenes.summary: A storm drives them for three days to the Strophades, where the Harpies foul their feast. Celæno prophesies they will eat their tables before building their city. They sail past Ithaca to Actium and Epirus.
scenes.stakes: The Trojans are menaced by the Harpies' curse and the loss of their fated city.

scenes.title: Andromache at Buthrotum
scenes.summary: Æneas finds Andromache mourning at a false tomb of Hector. She tells of Pyrrhus' death and Helenus' rule, and Helenus welcomes the Trojans.
scenes.stakes: Andromache lives in grief for Hector; Æneas hopes for news of kin and friends.

scenes.title: Helenus' prophecy and farewells
scenes.summary: Helenus prophesies the sow omen, the dangers of Scylla and Charybdis, and the Sibyl of Cumæ, and urges worship of Juno. Gifts and farewells follow.
scenes.stakes: Æneas needs guidance to avoid the perils between him and Italy.

scenes.title: Sighting Italy and passing Charybdis
scenes.summary: They sail to Italy, see the omen of white horses, and then turn from Scylla and Charybdis and are driven toward Ætna.
scenes.stakes: The fleet risks being swallowed by Charybdis and wrecked on the rocks.

scenes.title: Achemenides and the Cyclops
scenes.summary: Achemenides, left behind by Ulysses, begs rescue and tells of Polyphemus. The blinded giant appears and the Trojans flee.
scenes.stakes: The Trojans risk being devoured by the Cyclops, and Achemenides faces death.

place.name: Land of the Cyclops, by Ætna

scenes.title: Around Sicily; Anchises dies
scenes.summary: They sail round Sicily's coast to Drepanum, where Anchises dies. Æneas ends his tale.
scenes.stakes: Æneas loses his father, his guide and comfort.

alias_notes.explanation: Phœbus is a title of Apollo.
Pyrrhus, Achilles' son, is also called Neoptolemus.

notable_quotes.reason: Famous cry against greed: 'auri sacra fames'.
Æneas contrasts his endless wandering with Helenus' settled rest.
Polydorus' voice from the bleeding tree is a haunting scene.

analysis.text: Æneas' wanderings test his piety and obedience to fate; misreadings of oracles show that destiny is revealed gradually.
The book weaves Greek myth and Mediterranean geography into Rome's origin story, linking Rome to Troy for Augustan Rome.

legacy.text: Dante's Inferno echoes the bleeding tree of Polydorus in the wood of the suicides.
The phrase 'auri sacra fames' became a proverb for the lust for gold.

fun_facts.text: Virgil's Scylla, with dolphin tails and wolves' heads, is a version of the monster from Homer's Odyssey.

language_notes.text: "After that it had seemed well" is a long temporal clause; the main verb, "we are driven by auguries," comes only after it. Asia means the Trojan realm in Asia Minor.
"Erewhile" means formerly, some time ago. Lycurgus was a legendary savage Thracian king.
Æneadæ means "the people of Æneas," the name given to the new settlement and its people.
Gradivus is a title of Mars, the war-god, who was patron of Thrace.
"No alien" means Polydorus is Trojan-born and a kinsman of Æneas, so the blood is of his own people.
The spears that pierced Polydorus's body took root and grew into the thicket; his murderers' weapons became the bushes Æneas pulled.
Manes are the spirits of the dead; the altars, dark fillets (ribbons) and cypress were standard funeral marks.
"The main" means the open sea.
The island is Delos; the mother of the Nereids is Doris, and the Ægean's god is Neptune. Delos was sacred to Apollo.
Delos was said to float until Apollo, the "heavenly archer," fixed it; "filial gratitude" refers to his birth there, honoring his mother Latona.
Pergamus was the citadel of Troy; the new settlement is called its "second" Pergamus. Danaans means Greeks.
"Vouchsafe" means graciously grant.
"Methought" is archaic for "it seemed to me." The tripod was the seat of the oracle's priestess.
Teucer was a legendary early king of the Troad, so Anchises traces the Trojans' origin to Crete.
The mother is Cybele, whose worship involved the Corybantes, her attendants, and lions drawing her chariot.
Idomeneus, king of Crete, fought at Troy; he was driven out by his own people, according to later tradition, so Crete seemed empty of rulers.
"Bacchant mountains": Naxos was associated with Bacchus (Dionysus), god of wine, whose worshippers were called bacchants.
"Curetes": the legendary early inhabitants of Crete, linked with the infant Jupiter; here a name for Crete itself.
Pergamia echoes Pergamum, the citadel of Troy; the settlers name their new city after their lost one.
Sirius is the Dog Star, whose rising in summer was believed to bring scorching heat and disease.
"Methought": archaic for "it seemed to me"; it marks the vision as a dream.
"Delian god": Apollo, born on Delos, whose oracle had earlier sent the Trojans on their search.
Hesperia, "western land", is the Greek name for Italy; the Œnotrians were an early people of southern Italy.
Dardanus, founder of the Trojan line, was said to have come from Italy; Iasius was his brother.
Anchises admits he had confused the ancestral homelands, Crete and Italy, when he first read the oracle.
Cassandra, Trojan prophetess, was fated never to be believed, though she foretold the Trojans' future correctly.
Palinurus is Æneas' helmsman; "owns" means admits. Even the expert navigator loses his bearings.
Phineus was a Thracian king tormented by the Harpies, who snatched his food until the Argonauts drove them off to these islands.
"Sons of Laomedon" calls the Trojans heirs of a king famous for breaking promises, an insult implying treachery.
The prophecy of eating their tables puzzles the Trojans here; it is later fulfilled when they eat bread platters in Italy.
Ithaca was Ulysses' home; the Trojans curse him as the cunning Greek who helped destroy Troy.
Lustrations are purification rites performed with sacrifice.
Abas was a Greek warrior whose shield Æneas had taken at Troy; "Danaan" means Greek.
"Past belief" means incredible; the rumour concerns Trojans now ruling in Greek lands.
A mock Simois: a small stream named after the Trojan river Simois, part of the replica Troy Helenus has built.
"Goddess-born" addresses Æneas as son of Venus; she asks whether he is alive or a ghost.
Priam's virgin daughter is Polyxena, sacrificed at Achilles' tomb after Troy fell.
Hermione, daughter of Helen (Leda's daughter) and Menelaus of Sparta, was the bride Pyrrhus sought.
Orestes had been promised Hermione; he kills Pyrrhus (Neoptolemus) at the altar, at Delphi in tradition.
Zanthus is the Trojan river Xanthus; the Scæan gate was Troy's famous main gate.
Celæno is the Harpy who earlier prophesied that the Trojans would be driven by hunger to eat their tables before reaching their promised city.
Trinacrian means Sicilian (Trinacria, 'three-cornered island'). The spectral lake is Avernus; Circe's isle lies off the Italian coast.
Gnawing your tables refers to Celæno's prophecy that the Trojans would eat their tables; Helenus says it need not be feared.
Pelorus is the northeastern cape of Sicily, at the narrow strait; the left shore means passing round Sicily's coast, avoiding the strait.
The description is compressed: Scylla's upper body is a woman's, her lower body a sea-monster's with dolphin tails and wolf heads at the belly.
The Sibyl wrote her oracles on leaves, which lay in order until the opened door's draught scattered them.
Astyanax was the infant son of Hector and Andromache, killed by the Greeks after Troy fell.
Xanthus was the river near Troy; Andromache and Helenus have built a small replica of Troy in Epirus.
Ceraunia is the Ceraunian mountains on the coast of Epirus; from there the crossing to Italy is shortest.
"Cast lots for the oars" means they assigned rowing duties by lot, so those not chosen could rest.
"Night's car" pictures night as a chariot driven round the sky by the Hours; it is not yet midnight.
White horses are the first omen Aeneas sees on reaching Italy; Anchises reads them as signs of both war and peace.
Helenus, the Trojan prophet-king in Epirus, had told Aeneas to honour Juno of Argos on arriving in Italy.
Scylaceum is called "wrecker of ships" because of its dangerous coast; it is not the monster Scylla.
They steer left, away from Charybdis, by holding to the Italian side; the sentence says the whole fleet depends on this course.
Enceladus was a Giant defeated by the gods; in this legend he lies buried under Ætna, and his movements cause eruptions and earthquakes.
Trinacria is the ancient name for Sicily, meaning 'three-cornered' island.
Dardan and Teucrians both mean Trojans. Dardan comes from the ancestor Dardanus, and Teucrian from King Teucer.
Danaan means Greek, after the Danai, one of Homer's names for the Greeks.
The 'powerful pledge' is the clasp of Anchises' right hand, a binding sign of safety and good faith.
Cornels are the fruit of the cornel (dogwood) tree, small, sour red berries.
Jupiter's oak and Diana's cypress-grove are sacred woods; the comparison makes the Cyclopes seem a towering, awesome forest.
Helenus, the Trojan seer in Epirus, had warned Æneas to avoid the passage between Scylla and Charybdis and to sail round Sicily.
Legend says the river Alpheus in Elis (Greece) flowed under the sea to rise as the spring Arethusa in Ortygia, Sicily, mingling its waters there.
"Obedient to command" refers to earlier divine instructions, given through Helenus, to honour the gods of the places they pass.
An oracle forbade disturbing Camarina's marsh; the city's people drained it anyway and suffered for it, which gave rise to the proverb about not moving Camarina.
"Acragas" is the Greek city of Agrigentum on Sicily's south coast, famed for its horses.
"Pick my way" means steer carefully; the "sunk rocks" are hidden reefs near Lilybæum, the western cape of Sicily.
Helenus the seer and the Harpy Celæno had both prophesied Æneas's trials earlier in Book 3, yet neither mentioned his father's death.

context_notes.text: Antandros was a port at the foot of Mount Ida, in the Troad, where timber for ships was cut.
Dione's daughter is Venus, Æneas's mother; she was the divine patroness of his line.
Priam sent his youngest son Polydorus with gold to the Thracian king for safety during the war.
The "senate" is the council of Trojan elders, with Anchises at its head.
Anius was the legendary king of Delos and priest of Apollo (Phœbus). Fillets are ritual headbands.
Dardanus was the ancestral founder of the Trojan line, so "old mother" refers to the land of their origin.
Jove, king of the gods, was said to have been raised on Crete.
Sacrifices were colour-matched to the deity: black for stormy powers, white for gentle winds.
The Penates, household gods, were small images Æneas carried from burning Troy; Romans honoured such gods at every hearth.
A libation was wine, milk or water poured out as an offering to the gods, here on the hearth altar.
Without sun or stars, ancient sailors could not navigate, so storms were especially deadly.
Harpies were winged female monsters, snatchers of food, here half-woman and half-bird.
Misenus is the Trojan trumpeter; his name later marks a cape in Italy where he dies.
Celæno claims to be a Fury and to speak from Apollo's prophecy, giving her words divine authority.
Wrestling matches and games were a traditional way to give thanks and celebrate after danger.
Helenus, a Trojan prophet, was taken captive by the Greeks and later received Pyrrhus' widow Andromache and part of his kingdom.
Andromache was Hector's widow; the empty tomb (cenotaph) let her honour him though his body lay in Troy.
Neoptolemus is another name for Pyrrhus, son of Achilles.
Helenus, a son of Priam, was a prophet who now rules part of Epirus. Phœbus (Apollo) is the god of prophecy.
These are Greek colonies in southern Italy founded by heroes returning from the Trojan War, such as Idomeneus and Philoctetes.
Covering the head during sacrifice was a Roman rite; it kept ill-omened sights away. Virgil connects it to Roman religion.
Juno is hostile to the Trojans throughout the poem, so winning her favour matters most.
Neoptolemus was Achilles' son, who killed Priam. Andromache was later given to him, then married Helenus, so these arms are gifts from the former enemy.
Arcturus, the Hyades, the Bears and Orion are constellations used by ancient sailors for navigation and weather prediction.
Achates is Aeneas's faithful companion, here the first to spot Italy.
Minerva (the Greek Pallas Athena) is goddess of wisdom and war, so her temple suits the omen of war.
Tarentum was a Greek colony in southern Italy, and legend linked it with Hercules.
Ætna is the volcano of Sicily, here called by the old name Trinacria for the island.
Ulysses, king of Ithaca, blinded Polyphemus in Homer's Odyssey; Achemenides is a Greek sailor from his crew abandoned on the island.
Pelorus is the northeastern cape of Sicily, near the strait of Messina; the north wind carries the Trojans south along the coast.
Anchises, Æneas's aged father, was carried from burning Troy on his son's shoulders and has travelled with him throughout the wanderings.
Æneas has been telling his story to Dido and her court at Carthage; this closes his narrative of Books 2 and 3.

literary_notes.text: "An evil hour" hints that this settlement will fail, before the horror is revealed.
Physical terror is heightened through freezing, palsied limbs and curdling blood, showing the force of the omen.
Æneas's question, "ought I to tell the tale or hold my peace?", builds suspense and shows how awful the event is.
The narrator suddenly addresses gold itself, condemning greed with a moral outcry.
The island is made to "laugh at the winds," as if it could scorn them now that it is fixed.
The trembling of the temple signals divine presence and prepares for the oracle's pronouncement.
The oracle's vague "old mother" is misread by Anchises as Crete, which will later prove mistaken.
Anchises is shown as the wise elder who interprets tradition, though his reading proves fallible.
Catalogue of islands and the phrase "sprinkled over the waves" paint the Aegean vividly and convey the length of the voyage.
Just as the settlers are building laws, homes and marriages, plague strikes suddenly, undoing their hopeful beginning.
The gods promise imperial sway for Æneas' descendants, pointing ahead to Rome's rise.
Æneas insists it was no mere dream, showing his piety and the vision's authority.
Anchises' questions lament Cassandra's fate of being disbelieved and justify accepting her prophecy now.
Repeated "on every side" conveys the vast, featureless emptiness surrounding the ships.
"Blind waters" transfers blindness to the sea, mirroring the sailors' helpless wandering.
The claim that no worse plague ever left the Styx stresses the Harpies' horror.
"Again" echoes the earlier attack, creating a sense of a cycle of harassment.
Celæno's curse anticipates the later fulfillment of eating their tables in Italy.
Terror that "curdled their blood" shows fear physically transforming the men.
The green mound, two altars and shade-calling create a vivid, pitiful picture of grief kept alive through imitation.
Quick clauses without connectives mimic Andromache's shock, as she freezes, loses her warmth and faints.
Andromache calls the sacrificed Polyxena most blessed, reversing normal values to show how terrible her own slavery is.
The miniature Troy, with its copied river and gate, shows exiles trying to rebuild a lost homeland, a recurring theme.
The white sow with thirty piglets foretells the site of Alba Longa, and the thirty years before it is founded.
Charybdis lashing the stars with spray exaggerates the whirlpool's power to show its terror.
Repeated 'if' clauses and 'Juno, great Juno' stress the urgency and solemnity of the warning.
Fortune is a book whose pages Aeneas must keep turning, expressing his unfinished, uncertain journey against the settled lives of Helenus and Andromache.
Aeneas's hope of two kindred cities becoming one Troy anticipates the future Roman empire and its Trojan heritage.
Sleep is imagined as dew falling on tired limbs, giving rest a gentle, refreshing touch.
Aurora, the dawn, appears as a goddess reddening the sky, marking the moment Italy comes into view.
Anchises' reading of the horses as war foretells the conflict Aeneas will face in Italy.
Rising to heaven and sinking to the place of death contrasts the wave's extremes and conveys the ships' peril.
The Enceladus legend personifies the volcano as a buried giant, turning eruption and earthquake into a living, suffering body.
Night 'keeping the moon in a prison of storm-clouds' pictures the clouds as jailers, deepening the sense of dread.
Famine is imagined as an artist whose 'master-stroke' completes the man's wretched appearance, stressing his starvation.
'The brain of Ithaca' praises Ulysses' cunning by naming him for his homeland, and the single eye is vividly dwelt upon.
The Cyclopes are compared to oaks and cypresses in a sacred forest, conveying their height, stillness and menace.
Repeating Achemenides' name and the phrase 'ill-starred Ulysses' echoes the opening of his tale and closes the episode in a ring.
Æneas turns to address his dead father directly, heightening the grief and making the loss feel immediate.
The goal of his long journeys is described as a death, not an arrival; the loss is bitterly out of proportion to the hardships survived.
The poet returns from Æneas's first-person tale to the frame narrative, calmly closing the book with the hush of the listening court.
